title: I will not forget thee (Isaiah 49:15)
hookLine: even if a mother could forget her child, God will not

cards: "But Zion said, The LORD hath forsaken me, and my Lord hath forgotten me." Isaiah gives the city a voice, and that's what she says. Not a polite question.

A charge: you left, you forgot. It's the voice of someone who has waited by the phone so long that waiting has turned into certainty. The chapter doesn't scold her for saying it, or tell her she's wrong to feel it.
It answers her, and the answer reaches for the closest bond anyone knows.

teach.h: A NURSING MOTHER AND HER CHILD.
teach.b: The answer comes as a question: "Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee." Look at the image God chooses.
Not a king remembering a subject, or a master a servant: a nursing mother and her baby.
Then the surprising honesty: yea, they may forget. The verse admits that even the strongest human bond can fail. Mothers can be overwhelmed, or ill, or gone.
The prophet reaches for the strongest bond he knows, and then has God say that even if that bond fails, this one holds.

teach.h: GRAVEN ON THE PALMS OF MY HANDS.
teach.b: The next verse gives a picture you can almost hold: "Behold, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands." Graven, engraved, cut in. Not a note on a scrap of paper that can be lost.
Written into the hand itself, the way someone writes on their palm so they'll see it every time they reach for anything.

teach.h: THY WALLS ARE CONTINUALLY BEFORE ME.
teach.b: Thy walls are continually before me: Zion's broken walls, always in view. For people who felt erased by exile, this is the reply: you are not a name on a list somewhere. You are in the palm.
Jewish tradition reads these chapters in the weeks of comfort after mourning. The complaint is allowed.

teach.h: YET WILL I NOT FORGET THEE.
teach.b: And the answer is: I will not forget thee.

how: Jews read Isaiah 49 among the prophetic readings of comfort in the weeks after Tisha B'Av, and visiting the sick, bikur cholim, is counted in Jewish life as a mitzvah.

games.q: I will not forget thee — tap the pairs.

s: in Isaiah 49, Zion is scolded for complaining
the chapter answers her complaint instead of scolding it.
the verse admits a mother may forget
yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee.
Zion is written on a scroll in heaven
graven upon the palms of my hands.

games.q: you're the prophet. the city cries: the Lord hath forsaken me, and my Lord hath forgotten me. how do you answer?
o: tell her she brought it on herself.
say even a mother may forget, yet God will not.
tell her to stop feeling that way.
games.why: "yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee." the answer reaches for a mother's bond, and then goes past it.

practice: Let your mind go to someone who has dropped out of view: an old neighbor, a relative in a care home, a friend who stopped showing up and nobody asked why. Let their face come back, and say their name to yourself.
If you pray, you can hold the verse: I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands.

wordCard.voice: Zion, the city given a voice to say she'd been forgotten, and answered: even if a mother could forget her child, I will not forget thee.

orig.note: Hebrew: yet I will not forget you, from Isaiah 49:15.

carryVoice: Your line: you are in the palm. The week in Isaiah, line by line: here am I, send me; a little child leads; comfort ye my people; renew your strength; a light to the nations; the waters won't overflow. Until tomorrow.
